subject: Critical Thinking
title: Anchoring of First Impressions
description: A fast breakdown of Anchoring of First Impressions for builders.

hook.text: You meet someone at a party. They spill a drink on you.

buildup.text: First impressions form in milliseconds and persist for years. They anchor all subsequent information about that person.

discovery.text: Willis & Todorov: people form judgments of trustworthiness from faces in just 100 milliseconds – and rarely revise them.

twist.text: First impressions harden fast; interviewers often decide early and spend the rest confirming it.

climax.text: Awareness helps: consciously remind yourself that first impressions are snapshots, not films.

punchline.text: First impressions are fast, confident, and often completely wrong.

quiz.question: How quickly do people form judgments of trustworthiness from faces?

details.summary: Anchoring is the cognitive bias where the first piece of information encountered disproportionately influences subsequent judgments. First impressions set a mental reference point that is difficult to adjust away from.
details.whyItMatters: Anchoring affects negotiations, pricing, medical diagnoses, and legal sentencing, often without people realizing they are being influenced.
takeaways: Initial information sets a mental anchor that biases later judgments
Even irrelevant anchors influence decisions significantly
Awareness and deliberate re-evaluation help counteract anchoring

faq.question: How does anchoring bias affect salary negotiations?
faq.answer: The first number mentioned becomes the anchor. If a job posting lists a salary range, candidates tend to negotiate around that range rather than independently assessing their value.

faq.question: Can anchoring bias be eliminated with training?
faq.answer: Training reduces but does not eliminate anchoring. Even experts in a field are susceptible, though they may adjust further from the anchor than novices.
